sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This page is about Afghan Minnesotans: people born in Afghanistan or with family roots there. It includes families settled here for decades, students and professionals, the larger group that came after the Taliban’s return in August 2021 [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/), and U.S.-born children who may never have lived in Afghanistan.

### Who this is about, and who it is not

Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek, Turkmen and Baluchi people, Sunni and Shia Muslims, and small Sikh and Hindu communities all have Afghan roots [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/), and more than 30 languages are spoken [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf). A person from Iran, Tajikistan or Pakistan is not Afghan because of a shared language or border.

### How to use it

Treat this page as a starting point you test with the person. It cannot tell you what any one person believes, has lived through or wants, so ask.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Afghanistan secured independence in its foreign affairs from Britain in 1919, after three Anglo-Afghan wars between 1839 and 1919 [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf). The period that shaped today’s diaspora began with the April 1978 coup and the Soviet invasion of December 1979 [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/).

No single group is the nation. Minority Rights Group lists past survey estimates for Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek and other peoples, but states that no reliable current ethnic data exists, that the last official census was in 1979, and that intermarriage has blurred lines [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/). Ethnicity and religious community have shaped who was targeted in past conflicts, so they are not icebreakers. If a person names their people or province, note only what the service needs, such as language.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Afghanistan is landlocked and mountainous, bordered by Iran, Pakistan, China, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Pashtuns are concentrated in the south and southeast, Tajiks in the north, northeast and Kabul, Hazaras in the central Hazarajat and Kabul, and Uzbeks and Turkmen in the north, though people live across the country [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/).

The Afghan world also lies outside Afghanistan. UNHCR counts 2.6 million registered Afghan refugees, 2.2 million of them in Iran and Pakistan [UNHCR](https://unhcr.org/countries/afghanistan). Some Afghan Minnesotans lived for years in those countries; others passed through Qatar or the United Arab Emirates on the way here [Star Tribune 2025](https://www.startribune.com/some-afghan-allies-still-coming-to-us-but-with-less-support/601358694) [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/). Ask about past countries only when it serves the task, such as interpreter matching.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
Afghans have left across four decades: the Soviet war, civil war after 1992, the Taliban’s capture of Kabul in 1996, the 2001 U.S.-led intervention, and the Taliban’s return on August 15, 2021 [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf).

People came by different routes. Many 2021 evacuees arrived on humanitarian parole, which “is not an immigration status” [GAO 2025](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107433/index.html). Special Immigrant Visas serve Afghans with qualifying employment, with new Chief of Mission applications due by December 31, 2025 [State Department](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/us-visas/immigrate/special-immg-visa-afghans-employed-us-gov/afghan-faq.html). Others came as refugees or asylum seekers [Star Tribune 2025](https://www.startribune.com/some-afghan-allies-still-coming-to-us-but-with-less-support/601358694).

In January 2025 the federal government suspended refugee admissions and ended reception and placement contracts, and it moved to end Temporary Protected Status for about 9,000 Afghans [Star Tribune 2025](https://www.startribune.com/some-afghan-allies-still-coming-to-us-but-with-less-support/601358694). Status questions belong with qualified legal help.

sections.heading: Minnesota History
sections.body:
Afghan Minnesota predates 2021: Khyber Pass Cafe in Saint Paul has been open since 1984 [Sahan 2021](https://sahanjournal.com/helping-out/afghan-refugees-in-minnesota-how-to-help/). The community stayed small, with about 500 people of Afghan ancestry in 2021 [Compass 2021](https://www.mncompass.org/data-insights/articles/our-afghan-community).

In August 2021 Governor Walz offered to help resettle Afghans [MPR 2021](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2021/08/20/walz-extends-minnesotas-welcome-mat-to-afghan-refugees). From October 2021 through February 2022, 1,260 evacuees in 386 families arrived, in a response led by the DHS Resettlement Programs Office with the Minnesota Department of Health [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full).

The Afghan Cultural Society, founded in 2018, became a nonprofit in July 2022 and opened an office in Cedar-Riverside [Star Tribune 2022](https://www.startribune.com/afghan-cultural-societys-office-space-offers-hope-and-healing/600220249), where a resource hub opened on October 20, 2022 [MPR 2022](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2022/10/21/afghan-refugee-resource-hub-opens-in-minneapolis). TBS Mart and Afghan Darbar opened in Bloomington in July 2023 [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/).

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Households vary. In the 2021–2022 response the median family size was two, 47 percent of arrivals came as single individuals, mostly men, and the median age was 18 [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full). Some people are separated from spouses, parents or children still abroad.

Ask who the person wants in a meeting and who helps with decisions, then speak to the person directly. A relative’s presence does not authorize disclosure or decision-making by itself, so confirm the person’s wishes and any legal authority. Do not assume a woman needs a relative to speak for her, or that she wants to be seen alone; offer the choice.

The person caring for a child or adult with a disability may not be the caregiver on the form. Ask who does the care, and do not let “natural supports” quietly assign unpaid work.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Islam is Afghanistan’s principal religion. Minority Rights Group gives roughly 85 to 90 percent Sunni and 10 to 15 percent Shia, with Ismaili communities among Tajiks and Hazaras, and estimated Sikh and Hindu Afghans at about 900 people in 2016 [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/). Hazaras, largely Shia, have long been persecuted, including in attacks in Kabul in 2021 and 2022 [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/) [MPR 2022](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2022/10/21/afghan-refugee-resource-hub-opens-in-minneapolis).

Do not infer a person’s branch of Islam, observance, or religion at all from a name or ethnicity. Islamic food rules exclude alcohol, pork and meat not slaughtered by Islamic requirements [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf), so ask about food for events. If a faith leader or place of worship is involved, use the one the person names.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Dari and Pashto are the official languages [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf), both written in modified Arabic scripts [Microsoft Translator](https://microsoft.com/translator/blog/2020/08/17/translator-adds-dari-and-pashto-text-translation). MDH lists them as preferred languages among evacuees, with Hazaragi and Uzbek among less common ones.

### Commonly confused

Dari and Farsi are forms of Persian, but a Dari speaker may or may not understand Farsi well [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afghan.html). Translators without Borders calls them mutually intelligible in writing but very different spoken, recommends Afghan interpreters for Dari speakers, and notes that few Dari speakers command Pashto [TWB](https://clearglobal.org/farsi-and-dari-factsheet/).

### Booking

Book the language and dialect the person names, and orient interpreters to the person’s province [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afghan.html). Ask separately about written materials; Afghanistan’s national literacy rate is given as 38 percent [TWB](https://clearglobal.org/farsi-and-dari-factsheet/), which says nothing about the person. Use qualified interpreters, not children or coworkers.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Afghan names may not fit a first-middle-last database. Ask how the person writes their name, which part to file as the family name, and how to say it. Romanized spellings can vary across records, and family members may not share a surname.

Birth dates need the same care. AFP reported that the tazkira, Afghanistan’s main identity card, has had no date-of-birth field, that age has been judged from appearance, and that January 1 became a common recorded birthday, partly to avoid converting from the Solar Hijri calendar [AFP 2017](https://www.dunyanews.tv/en/World/421406-January-1-marks-mass-birthday-in-Afghanistan).

A January 1 date or a spelling mismatch is not a sign of dishonesty. Follow your program’s identity-verification and correction process, keep variants with their source where permitted, and never choose a birth date or surname for the person.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A service-provider backgrounder suggests greeting elders first, using the right hand to give or receive, and waiting to see whether a person of another gender offers a handshake, with a hand over the heart as an alternative. At holidays, people may say “Eid Mubarak” or “Nawroz Mubarak” [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf).

Let the person lead. If a hand is offered, take it; if not, nod and continue. Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and do not shorten a name for convenience. A U.S.-born young adult and a recently arrived elder in one family may greet you differently, and both are ordinary.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Tea is commonly served on visits [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf); accepting a little is fine, and you can keep to the purpose of the visit. In a home, look for shoes by the door or ask.

During Ramadan, a person who is fasting may ask for a different meeting time, so offer flexibility when asked. If someone misses an appointment, check transportation, work hours, the interpreter booking and whether the notice arrived in a language they read.

Afghan Minnesota is small, and people may know the interpreter or others in a waiting room. Explain who will hear what is said and how information is used, and offer a private room or phone option for sensitive topics.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
The Solar Hijri calendar has been widely used in Afghanistan, with its new year usually on March 21 [AFP 2017](https://www.dunyanews.tv/en/World/421406-January-1-marks-mass-birthday-in-Afghanistan); during their first rule, the Taliban imposed the Islamic lunar calendar [Newsweek 2003](https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna3067400).

- Nawroz marks the Afghan new year and spring, usually March 20 or 21.
- Eid al-Fitr ends Ramadan over three days, and Eid al-Adha coincides with Hajj [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf). Both Eids follow the lunar calendar, so their dates move each year.

The Afghan Cultural Society held a joint Nowruz and Eid al-Fitr celebration in Minneapolis on April 5, 2025, by its own account [Afghan Cultural Society](https://afghanculturalsociety.org/post/eid-al-fitr-2025). Ask which dates matter to the person before scheduling.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Educational histories range from university degrees to little chance at school, and access has differed between cities and rural areas [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf). Since the Taliban’s return, girls have been barred beyond primary school and women from university since 2022; UNESCO estimates 2.4 million girls are excluded from secondary education [UNESCO 2026](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/five-years-keeping-learning-alive-girls-and-women-afghanistan).

Nearly half of the 2021–2022 arrivals were 15 or younger [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full). The Afghan Cultural Society has helped families with school conferences and lists education mentorship [MPR 2022](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2022/10/21/afghan-refugee-resource-hub-opens-in-minneapolis) [HelpMeConnect](https://helpmeconnect.web.health.state.mn.us/HelpMeConnect/Providers/Afghan_Cultural_Society/Cultural_Organization/1). Hold IEP and evaluation meetings in the parent’s language, and do not read limited English or schooling as limited understanding of the child.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Minnesota screened 96 percent of eligible arrivals in 2021–2022. Of 1,020 with a full check, half reported at least one health concern and 56 percent were referred to a specialty; a women’s clinic used female providers and interpreters [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full). These figures describe that group at arrival, not Afghan Minnesotans now.

MDH guidance lists conditions clinicians may consider, including tuberculosis, dental disease and mental health concerns, and notes that parolees arriving after September 30, 2023, generally lack Office of Refugee Resettlement benefits [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afghan.html). MDH’s report on Afghan refugee children notes their resilience and advises against trauma screening at a first intake [MDH trauma report](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afgtrauma/about.html). No Afghan-specific Minnesota disability figures were found; do not borrow another community’s rates.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
LGBTQ Afghans live in Afghanistan and in Minnesota. Human Rights Watch reports that Afghanistan explicitly criminalized same-sex relations in 2018, that the Taliban kept the ban, and, from 60 interviews, that LGBT Afghans faced attacks and threats, sometimes with relatives informing on them [HRW 2022](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/01/26/afghanistan-taliban-target-lgbt-afghans).

Minnesota law differs: the Human Rights Act bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity [MDHR](https://mn.gov/mdhr/yourrights/mhra/). Use the name and pronouns the person uses, do not ask a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and do not share what a person tells you with relatives or community contacts unless a rule requires it.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Dress ranges from everyday Minnesota clothing to more conservative dress among some practicing Muslims [IRC](https://www.rescue.org/sites/default/files/2026-10/Afghanistan%20Cultural%20Backgrounder_0.pdf). Some women cover their hair and some do not, and dress tells you nothing reliable about faith, politics or wishes.

Dress has been political in Afghanistan. The Taliban’s August 2024 virtue and vice law requires women to cover their entire bodies, bars women’s voices in public and requires men to grow beards; the UN human rights office called for its repeal [UN News 2024](https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/08/1153631). A person who left under those rules may dress very differently here, or the same. Do not comment on dress or touch a head covering, and ask about staff and interpreter gender for exams or personal care.

sections.heading: Music, Literature, and Art
sections.body:
Rumi, the Persian-language poet and Sufi mystic, was born around 1207 in Balkh, now in Afghanistan [Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Rumi).

Music has been banned twice. Under the Taliban’s 1990s ban, many musicians moved to Pakistan and Iran, and music revived after 2001; after 2021 the Taliban banned it again, burned seized instruments in July 2023 and pushed hundreds of musicians abroad [RFE/RL 2023](https://www.rferl.org/amp/azadi-briefing-afghanistan-taliban-war-on-music/32513357.html).

In Minnesota, the Afghan Cultural Society keeps donated art, instruments, clothing and rugs for exhibits [Star Tribune 2022](https://www.startribune.com/afghan-cultural-societys-office-space-offers-hope-and-healing/600220249), and marked its new community center in 2025 with an evening of art and music [Afghan Cultural Society](https://www.afghanculturalsociety.org/updates). If invited, go as a guest; an event is not consultation.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Afghanistan’s men’s cricket team has drawn international attention. At the 2024 ICC Men’s T20 World Cup, it reached an ICC semi-final for the first time, losing to South Africa on June 26, 2024 [ICC](https://www.icc-cricket.com/news/trott-hopes-afghanistan-learn-from-semi-final-loss-to-achieve-greater-heights). No Minnesota source describing Afghan sports clubs was found.

Do not assume a young person plays any sport. If a family names a club or youth program as a trusted channel, treat it as one channel, not as language access or consultation.

sections.heading: Work and Business
sections.body:
Afghan Minnesotans work across many fields, and some held jobs with U.S. or international missions that qualified them for Special Immigrant Visas [State Department](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/us-visas/immigrate/special-immg-visa-afghans-employed-us-gov/afghan-faq.html). Businesses include Khyber Pass Cafe in Saint Paul and Ariana Kabob & Gyro Bistro in St. Louis Park, open since 2013 [Sahan 2021](https://sahanjournal.com/helping-out/afghan-refugees-in-minnesota-how-to-help/). Some Afghans moved here from other states for work and affordability [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/).

Recent arrivals face housing, job, banking and transit barriers with less federal help since 2025 [Star Tribune 2025](https://www.startribune.com/some-afghan-allies-still-coming-to-us-but-with-less-support/601358694). Do not infer a person’s past work from their pathway or current job. Ask about credentials when it serves a plan, and connect people to employment help where they qualify [DHS RPO](https://mn.gov/dhs/resettlement/).

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Start with language: confirm language and dialect, spoken or written preference, and any interpreter preference, including gender. The 2021–2022 response used Dari and Pashto interpreters with health backgrounds when possible [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full).

Do not ask a person how they left Afghanistan, what they saw or why they were at risk unless an authorized process requires it and trained staff do it. MDH notes that resettlement can bring racism, Islamophobia and providers’ “deficit mindset” [MDH trauma report](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afgtrauma/about.html). If someone chooses to share, listen and ask how they want to proceed.

Collect immigration status only when a program rule requires it. Welfare-system data on individuals are private [Minn. Stat. 13.46](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/13.46), so confirm authority before discussing a family member’s case, even a spouse’s.

sections.heading: Adjacent Communities
sections.body:
Some Afghan Minnesotans may connect with other pages here, but none substitutes for this one.

- Arabic-speaking Minnesota (arabic-speaking): Islam and Arabic-based script are shared, but Dari and Pashto are not Arabic [Microsoft Translator](https://microsoft.com/translator/blog/2020/08/17/translator-adds-dari-and-pashto-text-translation), so an Arabic interpreter is wrong unless the person asks for one.
- Indian (Asian Indian) Minnesota (indian): Afghan Sikh and Hindu families are Afghan [MRG](https://minorityrights.org/country/afghanistan/); do not reroute them because of religion.
- Somali Minnesota (somali): Cedar-Riverside hosts Afghan organizations too, and Islam is shared, but language, history and naming differ.

The app has no Iranian, Pakistani, Tajik or Uzbek page. A person from those countries who speaks Persian, Pashto or Uzbek is not Afghan by default; ask how they identify.

sections.heading: Counts and Statistics
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no Afghan profile; its ACS 2019–2023 table covers other communities [Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/cultural-communities), and a profile needs at least 175 unweighted records [Compass methodology](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/methodology).

- ACS birthplace: 332 Minnesotans born in Afghanistan in 2018 and 1,107 in 2022, table B05006 [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/). No margin of error was reported; check B05006 on data.census.gov for the current estimate and margin.
- Ancestry: about 500 in 2021, years and margin not given [Compass 2021](https://www.mncompass.org/data-insights/articles/our-afghan-community).
- Arrivals: 1,260 from October 2021 to February 2022 [Frontiers 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1413258/full); more than 1,300 from September 2021 to September 2022, per DHS [Sahan 2024](https://sahanjournal.com/changing-minnesota/afghan-refugees-immigration-minnesota-american-community-survey/).
- A reporter on MPR in 2023 cited census data showing more than 2,000, measure unstated [MPR 2023](https://www.mprnews.org/episode/2023/09/14/new-census-data-shows-persistent-disparities-for-growing-communities-of-color-in-minnesota).

Birthplace misses U.S.-born children, ancestry rests on self-report, and arrival counts miss later moves. Over 85 percent of evacuees lived in Hennepin and Ramsey counties [MDH trauma report](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afgtrauma/about.html).

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
- [Afghan Cultural Society](https://www.afghanculturalsociety.org/updates), Cedar Avenue South, Minneapolis. The state directory lists mentorship, health care navigation and mental health services in Hennepin and Ramsey counties [HelpMeConnect](https://helpmeconnect.web.health.state.mn.us/HelpMeConnect/Providers/Afghan_Cultural_Society/Cultural_Organization/1); 2022 staff spoke Dari, Pashto, Farsi, Uzbeki, Urdu and Turkic [Star Tribune 2022](https://www.startribune.com/afghan-cultural-societys-office-space-offers-hope-and-healing/600220249).
- [DHS Resettlement Programs Office](https://mn.gov/dhs/resettlement/): services for refugees, Special Immigrant Visa holders and Afghan parolees, and access to legal help.
- [Refugee and Immigrant Helpline](https://mn.gov/dhs/resettlement/helpline/), 1-800-814-4806, for navigation and referral.
- [MDH Afghan clinical guidance](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afghan.html) and the [CORE Afghan backgrounder](https://healtorture.org/resource/guide-afghan-backgrounder) for background reading.
- Agencies that have served Afghans include the International Institute of Minnesota, Arrive Ministries and the Minnesota Council of Churches [MPR 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/08/08/refugee-arrivals-fall-to-record-lows-in-minnesota). Check current services first.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Conditions keep changing. Refugee arrivals hit record lows after the January 2025 suspension; MPR reported in August 2026 that the International Institute had resettled 13 Afghan Special Immigrant Visa holders this fiscal year [MPR 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/08/08/refugee-arrivals-fall-to-record-lows-in-minnesota). MDH counted 4,602 primary refugee arrivals of all nationalities in 2024 [MDH 2024](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/screen.pdf).

Some families live with uncertain status, relatives at risk abroad, and the loss of careers, especially women whose schooling and work were cut off [UNESCO 2026](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/five-years-keeping-learning-alive-girls-and-women-afghanistan). Attacks on Hazaras in Kabul prompted a Minnesota vigil in 2022 [Star Tribune 2022](https://www.startribune.com/afghan-cultural-societys-office-space-offers-hope-and-healing/600220249). Do not raise these topics as small talk or read politics from ethnicity or faith.

Afghan Minnesotans built organizations and businesses quickly. Plan with them as partners, and pay community organizations for their time.

sections.heading: Connections to Human Services
sections.body:
### Language access

Book the language and dialect named, not “Persian” or “Afghan” [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afghan.html). Use qualified interpreters, follow CLAS standards, honor interpreter gender requests where possible, and never use children.

### Names, notices and outreach

Record names as the person uses them, keep variants with their source, and treat January 1 birth dates as ordinary [AFP 2017](https://www.dunyanews.tv/en/World/421406-January-1-marks-mass-birthday-in-Afghanistan). Offer key notices in Dari and Pashto with spoken explanation, reach people through more than one organization, and record who was reached.

### Greater Minnesota, disability services, workforce

More than 85 percent of evacuees settled in Hennepin and Ramsey [MDH trauma report](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/coe/clinical/afgtrauma/about.html), so a metro-only plan can miss the rest; check county data before assuming no Afghan families live elsewhere. Explain waiver steps in the person’s language, ask who gives care, and follow mandated reporting without treating a community as a risk. Afghan staff are colleagues, not the interpreter pool. Status questions go to legal help through the [RPO](https://mn.gov/dhs/resettlement/); civil-rights and eligibility decisions stay with the responsible office.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This page is about Minnesotans who trace their origins to Eritrea, the Red Sea country that declared independence in 1993 [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/eritrea/): people born there, their Minnesota-born children and grandchildren, and Eritreans who lived for years in Sudan, Ethiopia or elsewhere first. It is not about Ethiopians or about Tigrayans from northern Ethiopia, even though some share the Tigrinya language and the Ge’ez script.

Eritrea is plural. The U.S. State Department lists nine ethnic groups and Christian and Muslim populations of roughly similar size [State Department](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2120690.html), and arrivals span the independence war to the present. Treat this page as a starting point to test with the person. Ask how they describe themselves and which language they want, and let their answers correct anything here.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Italy unified Eritrea within its present boundaries in 1890, and Britain occupied it from 1941. In 1952 Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia, which eroded its autonomy over the next decade and absorbed it as a province. Armed rebellion began in 1961; the EPLF took control in 1991, and in April 1993, 99.8 percent of voters approved independence [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/eritrea/). Ruth Iyob’s [The Eritrean Struggle for Independence](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3474031W) (1995) covers 1941 to 1993.

Independence came out of about 30 years of war with Ethiopia, so being described as Ethiopian can matter a great deal to some people. Ask how the person identifies rather than inferring it from a language or a map.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Eritrea lies on the Red Sea, bordered by Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, with about 1,000 kilometers of coast and the Dahlak Archipelago. Asmara, the capital, sits in the central highlands; the western lowlands slope toward Sudan, and the coastal plain widens in the south into the Danakil [Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Eritrea). The south and center are mostly Christian and the north mostly Sunni Muslim [State Department](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2120690.html).

Up to one-third of the roughly 6 million people born in Eritrea live abroad, with large refugee populations in Ethiopia, Sudan and Germany [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). A Minnesotan may have grown up in Asmara, a lowland town, a camp in Sudan or Ethiopia, or another U.S. state, so ask where they lived before Minnesota.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
Eritreans have moved to Sudan since at least the independence war [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed at least 19,000 Eritrean soldiers [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/eritrea/). National service began in 1994 for men and women aged 18 to 40 and was extended indefinitely in 2002 [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). Human Rights Watch reports punishment of draft evaders’ relatives, no elections since independence and an unimplemented 1997 constitution [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea).

People have crossed into Sudan and Ethiopia, and some continued through Libya and across the Mediterranean. UNHCR counted more than 683,000 Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers in 2024. After war broke out in Tigray in 2020, Eritrean forces entered camps in Ethiopia and forcibly returned thousands. The United States resettled 2,400 Eritreans in fiscal year 2024 [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). Others come through asylum, family petitions or other states.

sections.heading: Minnesota History
sections.body:
A 2007 feature in Mshale, a Minnesota newspaper for African immigrants, reported that the Eritrean Community of Minnesota started in 1986 [Mshale](https://mshale.com/2007/03/01/eritrean-feature-story/print/). In 2008 several Eritrean Minnesotans at a human-rights talk declined to give their names because they feared for relatives in Eritrea [MinnPost](https://www.minnpost.com/perspectives/2008/08/twin-cities-daily-planet-eritreans-minnesota-weigh-dream-gone-mad/).

- The Eritrean Community Center of Minnesota is at 1935 University Ave. W., St. Paul [GiveMN](https://www.givemn.org/organization/Eritrean-Community-Center-Of-Minnesota).
- The University of Minnesota’s Eritrean Student Association relaunched in 2022 [Minnesota Daily](https://mndaily.com/city/new-student-group-celebrates-eritrean-culture/03/24/2022/snoadmin/).
- In 2021 a St. Paul school board winner was described as Minnesota’s first Eritrean American school board member [The UpTake](https://theuptake.org/meet-halla-henderson-minnesotas-first-eritrean-american-and-of-lebanese-heritage-to-win-school-board-seat).

Minnesota recorded 289 primary refugee arrivals from Eritrea in 2005–2019 [MDH](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2022/other/221369.pdf) and 117 in 2024 [MDH](https://www.web.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/24rhrpt.pdf). In January 2026 lawyers reported arrests of refugees in Minnesota, including Eritreans [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/ice-arrested-dozens-of-refugees-in-minnesota-and-sent-them-to-texas-lawyers-say/601564065).

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
No source used here describes a single Eritrean family form, and none should be assumed. Families are often spread across countries [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression), and relatives in Eritrea of people who evade national service have been evicted, cut off from rations or detained [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea). A person here may be supporting or worrying about relatives in Eritrea, in camps or elsewhere.

- Ask whom the person considers family and whom they want involved.
- Involvement does not grant authority to receive information or decide; follow the applicable consent rules.
- Do not use children to interpret.
- Different last names in one household are expected; confirm composition through standard verification.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Eritrea recognizes four religious bodies: the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Sunni Islam, the Roman Catholic Church and the Evangelical Lutheran Church [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea). There are no reliable affiliation figures; one 2020 estimate was 52 percent Muslim and 47 percent Christian, mostly Orthodox. The State Department describes Tigrinya speakers as mostly Christian, seven other groups as predominantly Sunni Muslim and the Kunama as mixed [State Department](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2120690.html).

Members of unregistered churches face arrest, and Jehovah’s Witnesses lost citizenship in 1994 [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea). Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians are among those who most consistently flee [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression).

Eritrean Minnesotans may attend Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, evangelical or Pentecostal churches or mosques, some shared with Ethiopians, and some are not religious. Fasting can affect meals, labs and medication, so ask, and do not infer faith from a name or region.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Eritrea offers elementary schooling in nine languages and three scripts: Tigrinya and Tigre in Ge’ez script; Bilen, Bidhaawyeet (Beja), Kunama, Saho, Nara and Afar in Latin script; and Arabic. Secondary school is taught in English [Leeds African Studies Bulletin](https://lucas.leeds.ac.uk/article/literacy-use-and-instruction-in-multilingual-eritrea-yonas-mesfun-asfaha-jeanne-kurvers-sjaak-kroon/).

- “Eritrean” is not a language. Ask which language, and which script the person reads.
- Tigrinya and Tigre are different languages. Tigray is an Ethiopian region, not a language. Amharic is different again.
- Tigrinya is also spoken in Tigray [EthnoMed](https://ethnomed.org/resource/tigrean-cultural-profile/), so an interpreter may be Eritrean or Ethiopian.
- If the person names Arabic, ask which variety.

Use qualified interpreters, as CLAS standards expect. In a small community some people worry about confidentiality or an interpreter’s background; ask whether the interpreter worked for them and honor a request for someone else without asking why.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Eritrea’s 2015 Civil Code gives each person a first name, a patronymic and a second patronymic, and allows a family name in place of the second patronymic [Civil Code](https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/legislation/details/22800). A second name is therefore often a parent’s given name, not a surname shared across generations. EthnoMed’s profile of Tigrinya speakers from Ethiopia notes that women there keep their names at marriage and that U.S. immigrants usually use the father’s or grandfather’s name as a last name [EthnoMed](https://ethnomed.org/resource/tigrean-cultural-profile/); confirm with each person.

- Ask which name goes in each field, and follow the person’s documents.
- Expect parents and children to have different last names.
- Record known spellings from Ge’ez or Arabic script so records match.
- Do not invent a family surname or treat a mismatch as fraud.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Greetings vary across ethnic groups, faiths and generations.

- Ask how the person wants to be addressed and how to say their name, then use it.
- Do not assume an Arabic religious greeting fits a Christian household, or an Amharic phrase fits an Eritrean one.
- Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and follow the person’s lead on contact.
- Greet the person you serve directly, even when a relative speaks for them.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Etiquette depends on the household, not the country.

- On a home visit, look for shoes by the door or ask.
- If food or coffee is offered, accepting a little is courteous; a person who is fasting may not eat with you.
- Ask before photographing or touching religious objects.
- Do not open with politics, national service or how someone left; some people have relatives at risk [MinnPost](https://www.minnpost.com/perspectives/2008/08/twin-cities-daily-planet-eritreans-minnesota-weigh-dream-gone-mad/).
- If an appointment is missed, check the time, transportation, interpreter, work and any fast or holy day first.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Eritrea’s 2026 public holidays included Orthodox Christmas (January 7), Timket (January 19), Coptic Good Friday and Easter (April 10 and 12), Independence Day (May 24), Martyrs’ Day (June 20), the start of the armed struggle (September 1), Ge’ez New Year (September 11) and Meskel (September 27), with Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha and the Prophet’s Birthday listed as tentative [timeanddate](https://www.timeanddate.com/holidays/eritrea/2026?hol=9).

Orthodox feasts and fasts follow the church calendar, Islamic holidays follow the lunar calendar and move earlier each year, and national days follow the Gregorian calendar. National days can carry pride, grief or disagreement, and not everyone marks them. Ask before scheduling around a date.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Schooling in Eritrea starts in the mother tongue, with English as the medium of secondary and higher education [Leeds African Studies Bulletin](https://lucas.leeds.ac.uk/article/literacy-use-and-instruction-in-multilingual-eritrea-yonas-mesfun-asfaha-jeanne-kurvers-sjaak-kroon/). A person may read Tigrinya in Ge’ez script, Kunama or Saho in Latin script, Arabic or English, or none of these well.

Human Rights Watch reports that students at the school in the Sawa military camp, some still children, are pushed into military service before finishing secondary school, and many drop out [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea). Years in camps interrupt schooling further. Others arrive with degrees that are hard to document.

Ask about schooling and literacy language by language. For an IEP or school meeting, book the parent’s language and do not rely on a student to interpret.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No Minnesota health rates specific to Eritrean residents were found, so none are given. MDH encourages refugees and other eligible arrivals to have a health screening within 90 days of arrival [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/guide/2assessment.html). Many people crossed the Mediterranean, which MPI calls the world’s deadliest migratory sea crossing [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). Do not ask a person to retell that journey.

Eritrea abolished female circumcision by Proclamation No. 158/2007 [Refworld](https://www.refworld.org/node/58404). In Minnesota it is a felony, and a parent’s consent is not a defense [Minn. Stat. 609.2245](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/609.2245). Do not assume anything from country of origin, and follow mandated reporting where a duty applies.

EthnoMed’s profile of Tigrinya speakers from Ethiopia notes that some women there prefer female providers for gynecologic care [EthnoMed](https://ethnomed.org/resource/tigrean-cultural-profile/). Offer same-gender providers and interpreters where possible, and ask about fasting before scheduling labs or medication changes.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Eritrea’s 2015 Penal Code criminalizes same-sex activity with five to seven years in prison, for women and men [Human Dignity Trust](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/eritrea/). Some LGBTQ Eritreans left because of that risk, and some are not out to family or congregations. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity [MDHR](https://mn.gov/mdhr/yourrights/mhra/).

- Use the name and pronouns the person uses.
- Do not share what they tell you with family, a community organization or anyone else unless a rule requires it.
- Offer a remote or different interpreter if the person worries about community ties.
- Do not ask a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender identity.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Dress varies by faith, group, age and generation. Some Muslim and Orthodox women cover their hair, and many people do not. Hair can carry meaning at celebrations; Bilen and Tigre women perform a dance that spreads their braided hair [Music in Africa](https://www.musicinafrica.net/node/15580).

- Do not comment on or rank head coverings or modest dress.
- Ask before touching hair, clothing or religious items.
- For exams, explain each step, offer a same-gender provider or chaperone, and let coverings stay on when possible.

sections.heading: Music, Literature, and Art
sections.body:
A 2025 UCLA dissertation describes guayla, with call-and-response vocals and a repeating rhythmic cycle, as a marker of Tigrinya identity and Eritrean nationhood in diaspora communities, distinct from the liturgical music of the Orthodox Tewahedo church [UCLA](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2207257c). Instruments include the krar, a five- or six-string lyre, and drums found among all nine groups, with dances tied to weddings and rites of passage [Music in Africa](https://www.musicinafrica.net/node/15580).

Victoria Bernal’s [Nation as Network](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL20348543W) (2014) studies how Eritreans abroad use the internet in politics and citizenship. Because music and flags can carry political meaning, ask the people taking part before choosing either for an event.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body: In 2024 the Eritrean cyclist Biniam Girmay won the Tour de France green jersey, the first African rider to do so, after three stage wins [Africanews](https://www.africanews.com/2024/07/22/tour-de-france-eritrean-biniam-girmay-wins-green-jersey). No Minnesota source found here describes Eritrean sports clubs. The June 2026 Eagan soccer tournament was run by the Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America [MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/06/30/ethiopian-soccer-tournament-draws-thousands-despite-immigration-fears); do not assume Eritrean families take part in Ethiopian events, or that they do not. Ask a young person what they enjoy rather than assuming cycling, running or soccer.

sections.heading: Work and Business
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no Eritrean profile [Minnesota Compass](https://mncompass.org/cultural-communities), so no employment or income figures are given. A 2007 Mshale feature described an Eritrean-owned restaurant in Minneapolis and Eritrean programs on community radio and cable access [Mshale](https://mshale.com/2007/03/01/eritrean-feature-story/print/).

National service has kept many people in unpaid government roles for years, and consulates expect emigrants to pay a 2 percent tax on income [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression). A work history may include service assignments, gaps or skilled work that is hard to document, and some people send money to relatives abroad. Ask about skills and credentials without assuming a level, and do not treat gaps as unreliability.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Caution about sharing information can have clear roots. Eritrean offices abroad control identity documents and expect emigrants to sign a “letter of apology” [MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/eritrea-refugees-repression), and relatives in Eritrea can face punishment [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/eritrea).

Minnesota’s data practices notice explains why data is collected, how it is used, whether the person must provide it, the consequences either way, and who may see it [Department of Administration](https://mn.gov/admin/data-practices/data/warnings/tennessen/). Use your program’s approved notice and explain it in the person’s language.

- Collect immigration information only when an authorized purpose requires it.
- Avoid questions about politics, national service or routes unless a required process calls for them.
- Ask about interpreter fit, preferred name and who should be involved.
- Refer status questions to immigration legal services.

Formal eligibility, accommodation and civil-rights decisions stay with the responsible office.

sections.heading: Adjacent Communities
sections.body:
An Eritrean Minnesotan may be filed under, or also identify with, other pages in this app. They are not interchangeable.

- **ethiopian, Ethiopian Minnesota:** Eritrea was federated with and absorbed by Ethiopia before independence [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/eritrea/); shared history does not make a person Ethiopian.
- **amharic, Amharic-speaking Minnesota:** some Eritreans speak Amharic, and a Worthington church serving Ethiopians and Eritreans worships in it [Worthington news report](https://www.dglobe.com/lifestyle/ethiopian-orthodox-church-almost-ready-to-build), but it is not Tigrinya or Tigre.
- **oromo, Oromo Minnesota** and **somali, Somali Minnesota:** neighboring peoples with their own languages and histories.
- **arabic-speaking, Arabic-speaking Minnesota:** relevant when a person names Arabic.
- **african-american, African American Minnesota:** some U.S.-born Eritrean Americans also identify as Black Americans; shared race is not shared history.

A Tigrayan from Ethiopia may share Tigrinya but not national history. Families can be mixed, so ask.

sections.heading: Counts and Statistics
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass profiles 27 cultural communities with 2019–2023 ACS data; Eritrean Minnesotans are not one of them [Minnesota Compass](https://mncompass.org/cultural-communities). No dated ACS birthplace or ancestry estimate with a margin of error could be read for this page, so none is given. Census table B05006 has an Eritrea row; check the latest five-year Minnesota release on [data.census.gov](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B05006?g=040XX00US27) and quote its margin of error.

- 289 primary refugee arrivals from Eritrea, 2005–2019, from 4 in 2007 to 50 in 2019 [MDH](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2022/other/221369.pdf).
- 117 in 2024, of 4,602 humanitarian primary arrivals statewide [MDH](https://www.web.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/24rhrpt.pdf).

Primary arrivals are people whose initial U.S. destination was Minnesota. These counts leave out moves from other states, other immigration routes and Minnesota-born children. They are not a population count.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
Organization descriptions are the organizations’ own.

- [Eritrean Community Center of Minnesota](https://www.givemn.org/organization/Eritrean-Community-Center-Of-Minnesota), St. Paul: connects Eritrean Americans to social services and culture.
- [Eritrean Community Radio, KFAI](https://kfai.org/program/eritreancommunityradio/): news and events on the Eritrean community in Minnesota.
- [Eritrean Student Association, University of Minnesota](https://mndaily.com/city/new-student-group-celebrates-eritrean-culture/03/24/2022/snoadmin/): open to Eritrean students at Twin Cities colleges.
- [MDH refugee health assessment](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/guide/2assessment.html) and [2024 Minnesota Refugee Health Report](https://www.web.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/24rhrpt.pdf).
- [Minnesota Human Rights Act](https://mn.gov/mdhr/yourrights/mhra/).

Ask each person which congregation, mosque or organization they use; no single organization speaks for everyone.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Eritreans abroad hold a wide range of views about their government, and diaspora politics can be tense. Do not ask about political views, and do not assume one partner represents everyone.

Optimism from the 2018 peace deal with Ethiopia has largely faded, and in early 2026 Deutsche Welle reported rising tension over Ethiopia’s push for sea access through the Eritrean port of Assab [DW via News24](https://news24.com/world/africa/port-assab-becomes-flashpoint-for-ethiopiaeritrea-relations-20260116-0415). Such events can affect a person’s worry and contact with family.

Proclamation 10949 of June 4, 2025 fully suspended entry of Eritrean nationals, with exceptions including lawful permanent residents and some immediate-family visas [Proclamation](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/DCPD-202500658/pdf/DCPD-202500658.pdf). Fear of enforcement may keep people from appointments; that is not noncompliance. Rules change, so refer questions to immigration legal services.

sections.heading: Connections to Human Services
sections.body:
### Language access

Book the language the person names, ask which script they read [Leeds](https://lucas.leeds.ac.uk/article/literacy-use-and-instruction-in-multilingual-eritrea-yonas-mesfun-asfaha-jeanne-kurvers-sjaak-kroon/), use qualified interpreters, and honor a request for a different interpreter.

### Names and records

Enter names as documents show them, record variations, and do not create a shared household surname.

### Notices and outreach

List Eritrean and Ethiopian communities separately. Work through the Eritrean Community Center, KFAI’s program and the congregations people name, and pay partners for their work.

### Greater Minnesota

Eritreans also live outside the metro, including Worthington [Worthington news report](https://www.dglobe.com/lifestyle/ethiopian-orthodox-church-almost-ready-to-build), so do not plan outreach only in the Twin Cities.

### Disability services

No Eritrea-specific disability figures exist here. Explain services and choices in the person’s language, and leave trauma history aside unless a service requires it.

### Workforce and assumptions

Eritrean colleagues are not the interpreter pool. Do not assume Ethiopian identity, refugee status, one faith or one view of the Eritrean government.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This page is about Minnesotans with roots in two countries, the Republic of Sudan and the Republic of South Sudan. They shared one state until South Sudan became independent on July 9, 2011 [Office of the Historian](https://history.state.gov/countries/south-sudan), and they are now separate countries with different histories, governments, majority languages and faiths. A person may be Sudanese, South Sudanese, both or neither, and only the person can tell you which.

### Who this is

Sudan holds more than 500 ethnic groups and 400 languages [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/); South Sudan has more than 70 languages, with Dinka and Nuer the largest peoples [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/south-sudan/). In Minnesota that range runs from Nuer families in Austin and a Dinka congregation in Rochester to Arabic-speaking professionals from Khartoum, recent arrivals from Darfur, and their U.S.-born children.

Treat this page as a starting point you test with the person. It does not describe any individual and never replaces asking.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
These are two states built over many peoples, so there is no single founding story. Sudan emerged from the Anglo-Egyptian condominium, and the United States recognized it on January 1, 1956 [Office of the Historian](https://history.state.gov/countries/sudan). Minority Rights Group estimates Sudan as about 70 percent Sudanese Arab and 30 percent African minorities, among them the Beja, the Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa of Darfur, the Nuba peoples and Nubians, and about 97 percent Sunni Muslim since 2011 [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/).

In South Sudan, estimates put the Dinka at about 35.8 percent and the Nuer at about 15.6 percent, with dozens of other peoples; no reliable census exists [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/south-sudan/). Ask which people, region and language the person names rather than reading identity off a country.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Sudan's regions carry different histories: Khartoum and the Nile valley, the east, Darfur in the west, and the Nuba Mountains and the "Two Areas" [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/). South Sudan, with its capital at Juba, lies to the south [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/south-sudan/).

Displacement added more places. By the early 1990s as many as half a million Sudanese refugees lived in camps in Ethiopia and Kenya [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/scholarship/historynuer), and many families still have relatives there. In Minnesota, the record below places people in the Twin Cities and in Rochester, Austin, Mankato, Faribault and St. Cloud, so do not assume Minneapolis.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
The war between the south and the Khartoum government began around independence; from the early 1980s it caused more than two million deaths and about four million displacements [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/scholarship/historynuer). From 1987 about 20,000 southern boys fled, many walking to Ethiopia and later Kakuma camp in Kenya, and close to 4,000 of these "Lost Boys" came to the United States in 2001 [International Rescue Committee](https://www.rescue.org/uk/article/lost-boys-sudan). A 2005 peace agreement ended the north-south war, and in January 2011 98.8 percent of southern voters chose independence [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/).

War continued in both countries, and people kept arriving in Minnesota as refugees, secondary migrants and other immigrants. Fighting among Dinka and Nuer members of South Sudan's Presidential Guard on December 15, 2013, became a civil war [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/south-sudan/). In Sudan, atrocities in Darfur date from 2003, and war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces began in April 2023; by October 2025 almost 12 million people were displaced, over 4.3 million abroad [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/).

sections.heading: Minnesota History
sections.body:
MDH records the first primary refugee arrivals from Sudan in 1985, with larger numbers from 1993 to 2006 and a peak of 143 in 1995 [MDH](https://health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/reftotals.pdf). About 400 Nuer settled in the Twin Cities in the 1990s, many after first living in other states [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/scholarship/historynuer).

- 1999: Nuer Community Development Services formed in Faribault; it is now based in Omaha [Post Bulletin](https://www.postbulletin.com/newsmd/south-sudans-nuer-tribe-seeks-community-center-in-austin).
- 2005: Zumbro Lutheran in Rochester opened its doors to a Dinka congregation [Zumbro Lutheran](https://www.zumbrolutheran.org/sudanese-dinka-congregation).
- 2013: Nuer and Dinka Minnesotans worked to keep South Sudan's war from crossing here [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/south-sudan-conflicts-haven-t-crossed-to-minnesota/237208441).
- 2023: Sudanese Minnesotans organized relief and evacuations from Columbia Heights [MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2023/05/01/sudanese-community-in-minnesota-fighting-for-loved-ones-caught-in-conflict).

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Carleton's study of Nuer Minnesotans describes kinship as the basis of community life and notes that refugees often lose those networks when they move [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/scholarship/nuercommunity). War also reshapes households: a grandmother may raise grandchildren, an uncle may be an adult's main support, and spouses or children may wait abroad. A 2025 report described a Minnesota citizen whose wife and daughters were waiting in Uganda [Sahan Journal via Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/visa-spat-travel-ban-add-new-uncertainty-for-minnesotas-sudanese-community/601346862).

Do not infer the household from surnames. Ask who lives in the home, who helps with care, and whom the person wants involved. For an adult, the person's choice decides who takes part, and formal authority is confirmed through documents. Program rules on household composition still apply.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Faith differs between and within the two countries: Sudan is about 97 percent Sunni Muslim with long-established Christian minorities [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/), while South Sudan's main faiths are Christianity, indigenous beliefs and Islam [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/south-sudan/). Do not assume a Sudanese person is Muslim or a South Sudanese person Christian.

The congregations documented in Minnesota sources are largely Lutheran. Carleton names Nile Our Savior in Faribault, with sermons in Nuer, and congregations in St. Cloud, Austin, Owatonna and Anoka, where Zion Lutheran ordained the first Sudanese pastor in the United States [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/sudanese-lutheran-mn). Zumbro Lutheran's Dinka congregation worships in Dinka [Zumbro Lutheran](https://www.zumbrolutheran.org/sudanese-dinka-congregation). Ask a Muslim person which mosque, if any, they want involved, and involve any faith body only at the person's request.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The country name does not tell you which language to book. Arabic is Sudan's only official language, and Nubian and more than 100 other dialects are also spoken [Minority Rights Group](https://minorityrights.org/country/sudan/). In South Sudan, English became official after independence but is almost no one's first language; Juba Arabic is a lingua franca with about 820,000 speakers, mostly as a second language; and Dinka, with five dialects, is the largest home language [USAID, 2021](https://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/PA00XFMT.pdf).

- Record the language the person names: Dinka, Nuer, Bari, Fur, Masalit, Sudanese Arabic or another.
- Dinka and Nuer are different languages. Juba Arabic, Sudanese Arabic and other Arabic varieties differ, so ask whether a given Arabic interpreter works.
- Ask whether the interpreter is a good fit, and change without asking why.
- Ask which languages, if any, the person reads.

The CLAS standards call for qualified interpreters, not untrained people or minors [HHS](https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards).

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two naming systems often meet here. Cultural Atlas, an Australian guide, describes formal Sudanese Arabic naming as a personal name, the father's first name and the grandfather's first name, with no surname; people abroad often adopt one for paperwork, and women traditionally keep their names at marriage [Cultural Atlas](https://theculturalatlas.org/north-sudanese-culture/north-sudanese-culture-naming).

For South Sudanese names it notes English first names, names from relatives or birth circumstances, and children called by a parent's name, such as "Nyan Deng," daughter of Deng, in Dinka; some people's middle name was recorded as a last name at immigration [Cultural Atlas](https://theculturalatlas.org/south-sudanese-culture/south-sudanese-culture-naming).

Ask how the person writes and says their name and which part belongs in the last-name field. Some records carry estimated birth dates, sometimes January 1; follow program rules on identity and do not treat an estimated date as a sign of fraud.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Greetings vary by language, faith, age and setting, so follow the person's lead. Cultural Atlas describes "As-Salam Alaykum" as the formal Arabic greeting in Sudan and suggests men wait for a woman to offer her hand [Cultural Atlas](https://theculturalatlas.org/north-sudanese-culture/north-sudanese-culture-greetings); its South Sudanese page describes handshakes as usual and titles for elders and teachers [Cultural Atlas](https://theculturalatlas.org/south-sudanese-culture/south-sudanese-culture-greetings).

A plain hello, your name and your role work in almost any first meeting. Offer a hand only if the person offers theirs, and ask how they would like to be addressed.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Introduce yourself, explain the purpose and length of the meeting, and check that interpretation is working before the substance. If a relative or elder joins, confirm with the person that this is their choice.

On home visits, ask about shoes, seating and photographs. If someone misses an appointment, check transport, work shifts, interpreter arrangements and family emergencies first; war at home strains Minnesota families [Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2024/07/18/sudan-war-impact-minnesota/). Never open with questions about the war or a person's ethnic group.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
South Sudan marks independence on July 9, the day in 2011 it became a state [Office of the Historian](https://history.state.gov/countries/south-sudan); Sudan's independence dates to January 1, 1956 [Office of the Historian](https://history.state.gov/countries/sudan). In 2016 the Star Tribune reported that Dinka and Nuer Minnesotans had marked independence separately the year before [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/south-sudanese-in-the-twin-cities-worry-about-fighting-in-their-homeland/386706281/), so do not assume one shared event.

- Ramadan and the two Eids follow the Islamic lunar calendar and move each year.
- Christmas and Easter follow church calendars.
- April 15, 2023, when Sudan's current war began [Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2024/07/18/sudan-war-impact-minnesota/), and December 2013 in South Sudan are anniversaries of loss for some families.

Ask which dates matter when you schedule.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Schooling ranges from university study in Khartoum or abroad to years of interrupted classes in camps. In South Sudan, English replaced Arabic as the language of instruction after 2005, and the 2012 General Education Act calls for local languages in early grades and English from Grade 4 [USAID](https://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/PA00XFMT.pdf), so a person schooled before then may have learned in Arabic.

An older Faribault Daily News report cited ACS data showing about 26 percent of Sudanese Minnesotans without a high school diploma [Faribault Daily News](https://www.southernminn.com/faribault_daily_news/sudanese-immigrants-make-their-home-in-rice-county/article_6249ed25-dcfb-57e3-83c6-b7d820cf9a03.html). That is dated and describes no family. Offer school documents and meetings in the parent's language, and do not use a child to interpret at an IEP meeting.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
MDH encourages refugees to complete a health screening within 90 days of arrival [MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/guide/2assessment.html). A small 1998 study of Sudanese refugees at a Minnesota clinic found high rates of prior infectious illness and communication barriers [University of Minnesota](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/sudanese-refugees-in-a-minnesota-family-practice-clinic/); read it as history, not a profile.

### Female genital cutting

UNICEF reports 86.6 percent of women and girls aged 15 to 49 in Sudan affected by FGM/C in its 2014 survey [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/sudan/reports/female-genital-mutilationcutting-and-child-marriage-sudan-are-there-any-changes-taking), and a national ban in July 2020 [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/sudan/reports/female-genital-mutilation-sudan). That figure is for Sudan only and describes no person. In Minnesota, cutting a minor is a felony, and consent is no defense [Minn. Stat. 609.2245](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/609.2245). Give care without assumptions and follow mandated reporting rules.

Offer mental health support plainly, without asking for a trauma history.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
LGBTQ Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans exist, and the laws they or their families left are harsh. Sudan's Penal Code criminalizes same-sex activity, with a maximum of life imprisonment after 2020 amendments removed the death penalty [Human Dignity Trust](https://humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/sudan); South Sudan penalizes sex between men with up to ten years [Outright International](https://www.outrightinternational.org/our-work/sub-saharan-africa/south-sudan).

Minnesota's Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity [MDHR](https://mn.gov/mdhr/yourrights/mhra/). Use the name and pronouns the person gives, keep what they share private, and ask about sexuality or gender only when the service requires it.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Dress and grooming vary with faith, generation and occasion. Faribault residents described keeping braiding, dance, music and cooking alive [Faribault Daily News](https://www.southernminn.com/faribault_daily_news/sudanese-immigrants-make-their-home-in-rice-county/article_6249ed25-dcfb-57e3-83c6-b7d820cf9a03.html). Beyond that, ask the person rather than relying on a general description.

Do not assume that a Sudanese woman covers her hair or that a South Sudanese woman does not. Height, scars or facial markings are not conversation openers and do not identify anyone's group. Ask before touching hair, clothing or the body, and offer a same-gender clinician or interpreter where you can.

sections.heading: Music, Literature, and Art
sections.body:
Worship music is the best-documented form in Minnesota. Carleton's archive holds a page of a Nuer-language hymnal from Nile Our Savior in Faribault [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/items/show/399), where sermons are given in Nuer [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/scholarship/nuercommunity); Zumbro's Dinka congregation worships in Dinka [Zumbro Lutheran](https://www.zumbrolutheran.org/sudanese-dinka-congregation). A Nuer hymnal is also a reminder that these languages are written and read.

If a family invites you to a celebration or service, you are a guest, not a researcher, and attending is not consultation. Ask before photographing anyone.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Basketball is the most visible sport in public reporting. Nuni Omot, who grew up in Minnesota after fleeing Sudan with family, started organized basketball as a junior at Mahtomedi High School and later played for South Sudan, which lost to Team USA 101-100 before the 2024 Olympics [CBS Minnesota](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/nuni-omot-south-sudan-team-usa-basketball).

That is one public story. Do not assume a tall child plays basketball, and ask how any youth program fits the person's plan.

sections.heading: Work and Business
sections.body:
The Faribault Daily News described Sudanese residents working as pastors, accountants, therapists and laborers, many in manufacturing and food processing, some running tax-preparation businesses, and people with degrees struggling to work in their field [Faribault Daily News](https://www.southernminn.com/faribault_daily_news/sudanese-immigrants-make-their-home-in-rice-county/article_6249ed25-dcfb-57e3-83c6-b7d820cf9a03.html). Austin's meatpacking economy drew families there [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/sudanese-newcomers-seek-community-space-in-austin/301321021/).

The Sudanese Farming Group, founded in 2022, brought 20 to 30 families together to grow crops such as jute mallow and okra in New Hope [MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/episode/2023/04/27/sudanese-farming-group-works-to-grow-culturally-relevant-crops-get-access-to-land). Ask about shifts before scheduling.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Get the language right first. Book the language the person names, not "Sudanese" or "African," confirm the interpreter's language and dialect before a complex meeting, and offer phone or video options. Never use a child as interpreter [HHS](https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards).

- Ask who the person wants in the room.
- Do not ask anyone to describe war, flight or losses unless an authorized process requires it.
- Do not ask about ethnicity to guess a person's side in a conflict.
- If someone shares something painful, acknowledge it and return to what they need now.
- Collect immigration status only when a program rule requires it.

Keep case notes to the least detail needed, such as "family emergency abroad."

sections.heading: Adjacent Communities
sections.body:
A person may also belong to, or be misfiled under, another page in this section.

- Arabic-speaking Minnesota (arabic-speaking): helps with Arabic access, but a person from either country may prefer Dinka, Nuer, Fur or another language, and Arabic varieties differ.
- Kenyan Minnesota (kenyan) and Ethiopian Minnesota (ethiopian): many South Sudanese lived for years in camps there, but camp years do not make a person Kenyan or Ethiopian.
- Somali Minnesota (somali), Oromo Minnesota (oromo) and Amharic-speaking Minnesota (amharic): separate peoples, languages and histories.
- African American Minnesota (african-american): shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

Eritrea, which has its own course in the app, is also a separate country. Use the page that matches what the person names.

sections.heading: Counts and Statistics
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no Sudanese or South Sudanese profile [Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/cultural-communities); it builds profiles only with at least 175 unweighted survey records [Compass methodology](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/methodology). Other counts measure different things:

- Refugee arrivals, 1979 to 2024: 1,161 from Sudan and 104 from South Sudan, including 59 and 43 in 2024 [MDH](https://health.state.mn.us/communities/rih/stats/reftotals.pdf). Secondary migrants are excluded, and South Sudan arrivals start in 2017.
- About 2,800 Minnesotans reporting Sudan as country of origin, per Census data cited in April 2024 [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/minnesota-groups-at-the-forefront-of-relief-efforts-in-sudan/600362134).
- More than 3,500 with Sudanese ancestry, per Census data cited in June 2025 [Sahan Journal via Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/visa-spat-travel-ban-add-new-uncertainty-for-minnesotas-sudanese-community/601346862); Neilsberg, a private data site, gives 3,588 for ACS 2019-2023, largest in Olmsted, Dakota, Mower, Hennepin and Blue Earth counties [Neilsberg](https://www.neilsberg.com/insights/lists/sudanese-population-in-minnesota-by-county/).
- Community estimates: about 2,000 Nuer in 2013 [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/south-sudan-conflicts-haven-t-crossed-to-minnesota/237208441).

None of these figures comes with a published margin of error, so treat each as approximate. Census categories can miss people who identify as South Sudanese or by ethnic group.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
- DHS Resettlement Programs Office and the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline, 1-800-814-4806 [Minnesota DHS](https://mn.gov/dhs/resettlement/).
- South Sudanese Community of Minnesota, Mankato, serving Blue Earth and Nicollet counties [Help Me Connect](https://helpmeconnect.web.health.state.mn.us/HelpMeConnect/Providers/South_Sudanese_Community_of_Minnesota/Cultural_Organization/1).
- Zumbro Lutheran's Dinka congregation, Rochester, in its own description [Zumbro Lutheran](https://www.zumbrolutheran.org/sudanese-dinka-congregation).
- Lutheran congregations with Nuer worship [Carleton College](https://religionsmn.carleton.edu/exhibits/show/os/sudanese-lutheran-mn).
- American Relief Agency for the Horn of Africa, Columbia Heights [Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/minnesota-groups-at-the-forefront-of-relief-efforts-in-sudan/600362134).
- Sudanese Farming Group, New Hope [The Food Group](https://thefoodgroupmn.org/farm/sudanese-of-mn).

Ask which organization, if any, the person uses before contacting one.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Federal rules for both countries have shifted. In April 2025 the State Department halted visas for South Sudanese passport holders, and a June 2025 travel ban included Sudan [Sahan Journal via Star Tribune](https://www.startribune.com/visa-spat-travel-ban-add-new-uncertainty-for-minnesotas-sudanese-community/601346862). Rules may have changed since, and status questions belong with immigration legal providers.

Staff do not referee homeland divisions that surface in Minnesota rooms: ask everyone the same neutral interpreter questions and never seat or assign people by ethnic group. Sudanese and South Sudanese coworkers are colleagues, not the interpreter pool.

sections.heading: Connections to Human Services
sections.body:
### Language and records

Record the specific language and dialect, not the country, so the person need not correct it at each contact. Records may show Sudan as birthplace for someone who identifies as South Sudanese, a middle name as a surname, or January 1 as a birth date; follow program rules for corrections and use self-identification fields.

### Outreach

Rochester, Austin, Mankato, Faribault, St. Cloud and the Twin Cities all appear above. A Minneapolis meeting and an English notice will not reach a Nuer family in Austin.

### Disability services and workforce

Explain waiver options in the person's language, include the supporters they choose, and allow time for family consultation without letting it override their decision. Accommodation and civil-rights decisions stay with the responsible office.

### What not to assume

Do not assume Arabic, Islam, Christianity, refugee status, recent arrival or a shared history. Ask.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This page is about Tibetan Minnesotans: people of Tibetan descent living in Minnesota, including elders who left Tibet, adults born or raised in exile settlements in India and Nepal, people who moved here from other states, and children born here. Minnesota is reported to hold the second-largest Tibetan American community, after New York ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/group/tibetan-american-foundation-minnesota-tafm)).

It is not about Chinese, Indian, Nepali or Bhutanese Minnesotans, even when a document lists one of those countries as a birthplace, and it is not about non-Tibetan followers of Tibetan Buddhism.

Tibetan Minnesotans differ by region of origin, dialect, country of birth, religious tradition, arrival period and generation. Use this page as background for better questions, and test each point with the person, who is the authority on their own name, language, faith and identity.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Ethnic Tibetans live across the Tibetan Plateau and parts of northern South Asia, and their written language has changed little since the seventh century ([University of Oxford](https://orinst.web.ox.ac.uk/tibetan)). In 1950 China’s People’s Liberation Army entered Tibet, and resistance peaked in a national uprising in March 1959 ([MNHS](https://mnhs.gitlab.io/archive/minnesota-immigrant-oral-histories/collections.mnhs.org/ioh/10000907.html)). The Dalai Lama fled to India that year, followed by more than 80,000 Tibetans.

The Dalai Lama established a government in exile on April 29, 1959, first in Mussoorie and from 1960 in Dharamsala; it is now the Central Tibetan Administration, and in 2011 the Dalai Lama handed political authority to an elected leader ([Migration Policy Institute](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/node/17894)). Tibet’s status remains a contested political question. Describe this history in sourced terms, and do not ask anyone to take a position on it.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Spoken Tibetan has three main regional forms, Central (including Lhasa), Khams and Amdo, which share a literary standard ([University of Oxford](https://orinst.web.ox.ac.uk/tibetan)). In exile, the first agricultural settlement, Bylakuppe in southern India, opened in 1961, and refugees later built 46 settlements; about 10,000 Tibetans now live in Nepal and 1,300 in Bhutan ([MPI](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/node/17894)). Many Tibetan Minnesotans were born in those settlements rather than in Tibet.

### Minnesota

The first arrivals in 1992 settled mainly in Northeast Minneapolis and Columbia Heights ([Northeaster, 2019](https://mynortheaster.com/news/local-tibetans-focus-on-future-in-northeast)). TAFM has centers in St. Paul and Isanti ([TAFM](https://tafm.org/about-us/)), and in 2018 it described a large Tibetan presence in the northwest metro ([CCX Media](https://ccxmedia.org/news/tibetan-group-wants-to-relocate-to-brooklyn-park)). Ask where a family lives rather than assuming one neighborhood.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
Tibetan Minnesota did not begin as a refugee admission. The Immigration Act of 1990 authorized immigrant visas for 1,000 Tibetans in India and Nepal ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/group/tibetan-american-foundation-minnesota-tafm)), awarded by lottery; each applicant needed a U.S. sponsor and a job, and at first only one family member could apply ([MNHS Becoming Minnesotan](https://mnhs.gitlab.io/archive/becoming-minnesotan/education.mnhs.org/immigration/communities/tibetan.html)). Relatives could follow after about three years. The recipients went to 22 cluster sites, and the Twin Cities was the largest, with 160 people ([MNHS](https://mnhs.gitlab.io/archive/minnesota-immigrant-oral-histories/collections.mnhs.org/ioh/10000907.html)).

### Later streams
